benchmark.goal: Which JavaScript runtime runs our short command-line scripts faster and with less memory: Node.js or Deno?
benchmark.scope: One process per run, start-up included, on a short CPU-bound script; not a measure of long-running servers.

reference_suites: none found for start-up plus a short workload; runtime vendors publish their own micro-benchmarks
pitfalls: code caches warm up after the first runs
a shell between hyperfine and the runtime adds its own start-up
Deno type-checks TypeScript files, so the workload is plain JavaScript

publication_terms.terms: MIT licence, with the licences of bundled third-party code

metrics.label: Wall time
metrics.definition: Elapsed time of one process running workload.mjs, start-up included, as measured by hyperfine without a shell

metrics.label: Peak memory
metrics.definition: Peak resident set size of the process, as reported by hyperfine

workload.description: workload.mjs builds 200,000 records, serializes them to JSON, parses them back, sorts and sums them
workload.usage_pattern: One short-lived process per script run, as in build and maintenance scripts

environment.background: Not controlled: a developer laptop with its usual background processes

runs.warmup: 3 untimed runs per runtime before each round
runs.order: 3 rounds of 10 runs; the order of the runtimes alternates between rounds, and hyperfine runs each runtime's runs consecutively within a round

limitations: One machine and one workload; a different script or a server workload may rank the runtimes differently.
Bun is not included: it was not installed on the measuring machine.
Within a round, the runs of one runtime are consecutive, so a slow drift of the machine can favour one runtime; alternating the order between rounds limits it.
